The talks follow a visit to the Dangote Industries complex in Lagos by an Egyptian delegation led by Mohamed Farid Saleh, the investment and foreign trade minister. Officials from Egypt’s Ministry of Petroleum and senior executives from its oil and petrochemical industry joined him. The group met Dangote executives to identify areas for industrial collaboration, investment partnerships and capacity expansion. Read also: Dangote Refinery crude deliveries hit record 735,000 bpd in October Egypt is emerging as a potential destination for future Dangote investments as the company pursues its Vision 2030 agenda. That strategy aims to widen the group’s presence across Africa, strengthen regional value chains and build a globally competitive manufacturing base on the continent. “This demonstrates true African integration,” Aliko Dangote, president and chief executive of Dangote Industries Ltd., said. “It reflects our belief that African businesses must invest across the continent to accelerate industrialisation and economic development.” Dangote said the visit let the group show the scale of what it has built while looking for ways to strengthen industrial capacity in both countries. Saleh said the mission was meant to turn diplomatic and business contacts between the two nations into concrete investments. The visit followed earlier meetings with Dangote Group at the Alamein Economic Conference and other investment forums hosted by Egypt, he said. Cairo wants to understand the capabilities Dangote has developed in refining, petrochemicals, fertiliser and related manufacturing, Saleh said. Read also: Dangote group performs excellently in driving economy – Tinubu “We are impressed by the scale of operations we have seen here—from refining and petrochemicals to fertiliser production,” he said. “Our objective is to identify areas where Egyptian and Nigerian businesses can collaborate, expand industrial capacities and create long-term value for both economies.” He said the private sector must lead any partnership. “By learning from each other’s experiences and combining our strengths, we can expand industrial production, encourage investment flows and create sustainable growth opportunities for our people,” he said. Saleh pointed to a combined market of about 400 million people in Nigeria and Egypt. He said Nigeria’s energy resources and Egypt’s established industrial base give the two countries a foundation for deeper cooperation in manufacturing, energy, petrochemicals and fertilisers. Closer ties could encourage Nigerian industrialists to expand into Egypt and give Egyptian companies more room to grow in Nigeria, he said. The benefits would go beyond trade and investment to include job creation, technology transfer, skills development and the growth of supporting industries, he added. Read also: Dangote-linked deal puts Nairobi bourse on track for first foreign inflows since 2019 Asked whether Egypt would welcome a Dangote refinery, Saleh signalled that the talks are not limited to that. “It doesn’t have to be a refinery specifically,” he said. “There are several sectors in which collaboration can happen. What is important is building a partnership that creates value for both countries and for Africa as a whole.” No investment amounts, timelines or specific projects have been disclosed. Beyond refining and petrochemicals, the relationship could open opportunities in fertiliser production, general manufacturing, energy-related investments and industrial services. The exchange fits a broader push by African businesses and governments to channel continental capital and expertise into regional industry rather than relying on outside investors. If the talks lead to deals, the Nigeria-Egypt partnership could serve as a template for that approach.
